title: The prophet prays to see the hidden things
source_text: Ἀλλὰ καὶ εἴπερ ὁ Μωϋσέως νόμος μηδὲν εἶχεν ἐγγεγραμμένον δι᾿ ὑπονοιῶν δηλούμενον, οὐκ ἂν ὁ προφήτης εὐχόμενος ἔλεγε τῷ θεῷ· „ἀποκάλυψον τοὺς ὀφθαλμούς μου, καὶ κατανοήσω τὰ θαυμάσιά σου ἐκ τοῦ νόμου σου.“ νυνὶ δὲ ᾔδει ὅτι ἐστί τι „κάλυμμα“ ἀγνοίας ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ τῶν ἀναγινωσκόντων καὶ μὴ συνιέντων τὰ τροπολογούμενα ἐπικείμενον· ὅπερ „κάλυμμα περιαιρεῖται“ τοῦ θεοῦ δωρουμένου, ἐπὰν ἐπακούσῃ τῷ παρ᾿ ἑαυτοῦ πάντα ποιήσαντι καὶ διὰ τὴν ἕξιν τὰ αἰσθητήρια γυμνάσαντι πρὸς διάκρισιν καλοῦ καὶ κακοῦ καὶ ἐν τῇ εὐχῇ συνεχέστατα φήσαντι· „ἀποκάλυψον τοὺς ὀφθαλμούς μου, καὶ κατανοήσω τὰ θαυμάσιά σου ἐκ τοῦ νόμου σου.“ τίς δ᾿ ἀναγινώσκων δράκοντα ἐν τῷ Αἰγυπτίῳ ποταμῷ ζῶντα καὶ τοὺς ἰχθύας ἐμφωλεύοντας αὐτοῦ ταῖς φολίσιν ἢ „ἀπὸ τῶν προχωρημάτων“ τοῦ Φαραὼ πληρούμενα τὰ Αἰγύπτου ὄρη, οὐ προάγεται αὐτόθεν πρὸς τὸ ζητῆσαι, τίς ὁ τοσούτων δυσωδῶν „προχωρημάτων“ αὐτοῦ πληρῶν τὰ Αἰγυπτίων ὄρη καὶ τίνα τὰ τῶν Αἰγυπτίων ὄρη καὶ τίνες οἱ ἐν Αἰγύπτῳ ποταμοὶ, περὶ ὧν αὐχῶν λέγει ὁ προειρημένος Φαραώ· „ἐμοί εἰσιν οἱ ποταμοὶ, καὶ ἐγὼ ἐποίησα αὐτοὺς,“ καὶ τίς ὁ ἀνάλογον τοῖς ἀποδειχθησομένοις ἀπὸ τῆς ἑρμηνείας ποταμοῖς δράκων καὶ τίνες οἱ ἐν ταῖς φολίσιν αὐτοῦ ἰχθύες; καὶ τί με δεῖ ἐπὶ πλέον κατασκευάζειν τὰ μὴ δεόμενα κατασκευῆς. ἐφ᾿ οἷς λέγεται τὸ „τίς σοφὸς καὶ συνήσει ταῦτα; ἢ συνετὸς καὶ ἐπιγνώσεται αὐτά;“ ἐπὶ πλεῖον δ᾿ ἐξέτεινα τὸν λόγον βουλόμενος παραστῆσαι μὴ ὑγιῶς εἰρῆσθαι τῷ Κέλσῳ ὅτι οἱ ἐπιεικέστεροι Ἰουδαίων καὶ Χριστιανῶν πειρῶνταί πως ἀλληγορεῖν αὐτὰ, ἔστι δ᾿ οὐχ οἷα ἀλληγορίαν ἐπιδέχεσθαί τινα ἀλλ᾿ ἄντικρυς εὐηθέστατα μεμυθολόγηται. πολλῷ γὰρ μᾶλλον τὰ Ἑλλήνων οὐ μόνον εὐηθέστατα ἀλλὰ καὶ ἀσεβέστατα μεμυθολόγηται. τὰ γὰρ ἡμέτερα ἐστόχασται καὶ τοῦ πλήθους τῶν ἁπλουστέρων. ὅπερ οἱ τὰ Ἑλληνικὰ πλάσματα ποιήσαντες οὐκ ἐφυλάξαντο. διόπερ οὐκ ἀχαρίστως ὁ Πλάτων ἐκβάλλει τῆς ἑαυτοῦ πολιτείας τοὺς τοιουσδὶ μύθους καὶ τὰ τοιαδὶ ποιήματα.
pass_a_gloss: But also if the law of Moses had nothing written in it made clear (δηλόω) through hidden meanings (ὑπόνοια), the prophet praying would not have said to God: 'uncover (ἀποκαλύπτω) my eyes and I will perceive (κατανοέω) your wonders (θαυμάσια) out of your law.' But now he knew that there is some veil (κάλυμμα) of ignorance (ἄγνοια) lying (ἐπίκειμαι) on the heart of those reading and not understanding (συνίημι) the figuratively meant things (τροπολογούμενα); which veil is taken away (περιαιρέω) when God gives it as a gift (δωρέομαι), when he listens (ἐπακούω) to the one who has done all on his own part and through habit (ἕξις) has exercised (γυμνάζω) the senses (αἰσθητήρια) for discernment (διάκρισις) of good and evil and says most constantly in prayer: 'uncover my eyes...' Who reading of a dragon (δράκων) living in the Egyptian river and the fish lurking (ἐμφωλεύω) in its scales (φολίς), or of the mountains of Egypt filled from the excrements (προχώρημα) of Pharaoh, is not led (προάγω) at once to seek who it is that fills the mountains of the Egyptians with such foul-smelling (δυσώδης) excrements, and what the mountains of the Egyptians are, and who the rivers in Egypt, about which the aforesaid Pharaoh boasting (αὐχέω) says: 'mine are the rivers and I made them', and who is the dragon analogous (ἀνάλογον) to the rivers to be shown from interpretation (ἑρμηνεία), and who the fish in its scales? And why must I further establish (κατασκευάζω) what needs no establishing? On which it is said: 'who is wise and will understand these? or intelligent (συνετός) and will recognize (ἐπιγινώσκω) them?' I extended the argument wishing to show that Celsus did not speak soundly (ὑγιῶς) that the more reasonable of Jews and Christians try somehow to allegorize them, but they are not such as to admit any allegory but outright (ἄντικρυς) are most foolishly (εὐηθέστατα) mythologized (μυθολογέω). For much rather the Greek things are mythologized not only most foolishly but also most impiously (ἀσεβέστατα). For ours have aimed at (στοχάζομαι) also the multitude of the simpler; which those who made the Greek fictions (πλάσμα) did not guard (φυλάσσομαι). Therefore not ungraciously (οὐκ ἀχαρίστως) Plato expels (ἐκβάλλω) from his republic (πολιτεία) such myths and such poems.
pass_b_english: Moreover, if the law of Moses had contained nothing written in it to be made known through hidden meanings, the prophet would not have said to God in his prayer: “Uncover my eyes, and I shall perceive your wonders out of your law” (Psalm 119:18). But as it is, he knew that a “veil” of ignorance lies upon the heart of those who read but do not understand what is said figuratively (2 Corinthians 3:15). This “veil is taken away” (2 Corinthians 3:16) as God’s gift, when he hears the one who has done all that lay in his power, who by practice has trained his senses to distinguish good and evil (Hebrews 5:14), and who says again and again in prayer: “Uncover my eyes, and I shall perceive your wonders out of your law” (Psalm 119:18).

Who, reading of a dragon that lives in the river of Egypt, and of fish lurking in its scales (Ezekiel 29:3–4), or of the mountains of Egypt filled “with the dung” of Pharaoh (Ezekiel 32:6), is not moved at once to ask who it is that fills the mountains of the Egyptians with so much of his foul-smelling “dung,” and what the mountains of the Egyptians are? And what are the rivers in Egypt about which this same Pharaoh boasts, saying, “The rivers are mine, and I made them” (Ezekiel 29:3)? And who is the dragon that corresponds to those rivers, as the interpretation will show them to be, and who are the fish in its scales?

But why need I establish further what needs no establishing? Of such things it is said: “Who is wise, and will understand these things? Or who is discerning, and will know them?” (Hosea 14:9). I have extended my argument at some length because I wished to show that Celsus was not right in saying that “the more reasonable among Jews and Christians try somehow to allegorize these things, but they are not such as to admit any allegory; they are plainly fables of the silliest kind.” For it is the stories of the Greeks, far more, that are fables, and not only of the silliest kind but also of the most impious. For our writings have had regard also for the multitude of simpler people, and this the makers of the Greek fictions did not take care to do. That is why Plato, with good reason, banishes such myths and such poems from his own republic (Plato, Republic 2.377b–3.398b).

doubled 'when ... whenever' removed: 'taken away as God's gift, when he hears'
παρ᾿ ἑαυτοῦ πάντα ποιήσαντι: 'done all that lay in his power' (was ambiguous 'in his own power')
τοσούτων ... προχωρημάτων αὐτοῦ: 'so much of his foul-smelling dung' (αὐτοῦ restored)
πολλῷ μᾶλλον clause reworded so 'far more' attaches to the Greek stories
Ezekiel 29:3, 29:3–4, 32:6 (LXX), 2 Corinthians 3:15–16, Hebrews 5:14, Hosea 14:10 LXX = 14:9 checked

Psalm 118:18 LXX = Psalm 119:18 English; τὰ θαυμάσιά σου ἐκ τοῦ νόμου σου rendered 'your wonders out of your law' to keep both pronouns. Hosea 14:10 LXX (and Hebrew) = Hosea 14:9 English. Ezekiel 32:6: the LXX reads 'the land shall be watered from your excrements (προχωρημάτων) ... upon the mountains', where the Hebrew has 'blood'; Origen follows the LXX, so 'dung' is kept. Ezekiel 29:4 LXX has the fish clinging to Pharaoh's 'fins/wings' (πτέρυγας); Origen says 'scales' (φολίσιν), following the Hebrew sense or his own paraphrase; cited as an allusion. 2 Corinthians 3:15–16 and Hebrews 5:14 are allusions woven into Origen's sentence, cited beside the words they echo. 'All that lay in his power' renders παρ᾿ ἑαυτοῦ πάντα ποιήσαντι (all that lies with him). The last Celsus quotation repeats his claim from 4.48–49; ἐπιεικέστεροι 'more reasonable' as in 4.48. οὐκ ἀχαρίστως rendered 'with good reason'. Plato's censorship of myths runs Republic 2.377b–3.398b (banishment of the imitative poet at 3.398a; again 10.607a).
